generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, self-efficacy decides whether you keep going on the parts of a subject that feel hard. Believing you can handle a specific task grows as you master small pieces of it, one at a time. Motivation matters too: a student who wants to understand the material tends to outlast one driven only by the next mark, especially when the work is demanding.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who face the same demanding task, one neither of them feels ready for.

Student A is driven mainly by the mark and has little belief in being able to do the task. The first hard question confirms the fear, and Student A concludes there is no point and hands in a thin attempt. Low self-belief and a focus on the mark alone made the task easy to abandon.

Student B also finds it hard, but starts by mastering one small part, then a second, building a sense of being able to do it. Student B wants to understand the work, not just pass, and asks someone who struggled with it last year how they got through. Belief and learning motivation keep the effort going to the end.

Both students found the task hard. Only Student B built the self-efficacy, and leaned on the motivation, needed to finish it well.
generatedProse.summary: What keeps you going on hard work is self-belief and the right kind of motivation. Self-efficacy is your belief that you can do a specific task, and it grows through mastery, seeing others succeed, feedback and managing stress. Learning motivation sustains effort better than chasing marks alone. You can now tell the two motivations apart and build self-efficacy on purpose. The last lesson turns this into goals.

check.body: In the worked example, how did Student B build self-efficacy for the task?

items.text: By mastering one small part, then another, and asking someone who had struggled through it.
By reminding themselves that the mark was all that mattered.
By deciding the task was simply not for them.
By handing in a thin attempt to get it over with.

feedback.correct: That's right. Mastering small parts and seeing someone like them succeed built Student B's self-efficacy.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the moves that gave Student B a sense of being able to do it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B built self-efficacy by mastering one part then another, and by asking someone who had struggled through it. The others describe low self-belief.
